title: A Podcast: The Future of Work

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Welcome to the WKU Student Podcast. Today we're discussing the future of work — specifically, how technology is changing the types of jobs that will exist in the next ten to twenty years. I'm joined by two guests. Amir, you study computer science. What's your view?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I think we're at a turning point. Automation and AI are already replacing a lot of routine tasks — data entry, basic customer service, simple manufacturing. The question isn't whether this will happen. It's already happening.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: And you, Zhibek — you study sports science. Do you feel affected by this?

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: Honestly, less worried than some. Physical training, coaching, healthcare — these involve human judgment and emotional connection. I don't think a robot can replace a good coach.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I agree that human connection is important. But I'd point out that AI is already being used in sports analytics — tracking performance, predicting injuries, designing training programmes. The role of the coach is changing.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: Maybe. But the coach who uses AI tools well will be better — not replaced. The tool enhances the human, not the other way round.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: That's an interesting argument. Amir, what skills do you think will be most valuable in this changing economy?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Critical thinking. Creativity. The ability to work with AI rather than compete with it. And languages — especially English — because so much of the important content and collaboration happens in English.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I'd add emotional intelligence and adaptability. The jobs that will survive are the ones that require you to genuinely understand and respond to people.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Do either of you worry about the social effects — job losses, inequality?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Yes. If automation creates wealth but doesn't distribute it fairly, we get more inequality. That's a political and economic problem, not a technology problem. But it's very real.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I think the education system needs to adapt much faster than it currently does. We're still training people for jobs that are disappearing.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Final question: are you optimistic about the future of work?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Cautiously optimistic. Technology has always created new jobs alongside the ones it eliminated. The challenge is the transition — making sure no one gets left behind.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I'm optimistic if education changes. If it doesn't, I'm worried. The choice is ours.
